wick.e: It has been suggested that noun etymology 1, noun sense 2 (“penis”) is derived from Hampton Wick, used as rhyming slang for prick. If so, that sense should be placed under etymology 2.
wick.g: A braid or bundle of fibre or other porous material (now generally twisted or woven cotton) in a candle, kerosene heater, oil lamp, etc., th

wick.e: From Middle English wik, wike, wich, wicke (“dwelling, home; building or land, probably enclosed, in which work is done; area, region, territory; city, town; hamlet, village”), from Old English wīc (“dwelling place, abode, lodging; temporary dwelling place, camp; place where a thing remains.
wick.g: A hamlet or village; also, a town.

wicked.e: From Middle English wicked, wikked, an alteration of Middle English wicke, wikke (“morally perverse, evil, wicked”). Of uncertain origin. Possibly from an adjectival use of Old English wiċċa (“wizard, sorcerer”), from Proto-West Germanic *wikkō (“necromancer, sorcerer”), though the phonology makes this theory difficult to explain.
wicked.g: Evil or mischievous by nature; morally reprehensible.

wickedly.e: From Middle English wyckedly, wykkedlyche, equivalent to wicked + -ly.

wickedness.e: From Middle English wikkednesse, wikkednes, equivalent to wicked + -ness.
wickedness.g: The state of being wicked; evil disposition; immorality.

wide.e: From Middle English wid, wyd, from Old English wīd (“wide, vast, broad, long; distant, far”), from Proto-Germanic *wīdaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁weydʰh₁- (“to divide, separate”), a dissimilated univerbation from *dwi- (“apart, asunder, in two”) + *dʰeh₁- (“to do, put, place”).
wide.g: Having a large physical extent from side to side.

widely.e: From Middle English wijdly, equivalent to wide + -ly.
widely.g: In a wide manner; across a wide area; to a wide audience.

wideness.e: From Middle English wydnesse, from Old English wīdnes (“width, wideness”), equivalent to wide + -ness.
wideness.g: The state or quality of being wide.

widow.e: From Middle English widwe, from Old English widuwe (“widow”), from Proto-West Germanic *widuwā (“widow”), from Proto-Germanic *widuwǭ (“widow”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁widʰéwh₂ (“widow”), possibly from *h₁weydʰh₁-, *widʰ- (“to separate, split, cleave, divide”), whence also wood from Old English widu, wudu.
widow.g: A person whose spouse is absent:

widowhood.e: From Middle English widwehede, equivalent to widow + -hood.
widowhood.g: The state or period of being a widow or widower.

width.e: From wide + -th (abstract nominal suffix), possibly by analogy with Old Norse vídd (“width”), though this is unlikely, as the word is not attested before the end of the 16th century and was historically unknown in Scots and the traditional dialect of Northern England.

wield.e: From Middle English welden, from the merger of Old English wealdan (“to control, rule”) (strong class 7) and Old English wieldan (“to control, subdue”) (weak). Both verbs derive from Proto-West Germanic *waldan and *waldijan, respectively; and are ultimately from Proto-Germanic *waldaną (“to rule”).
wield.g: To handle with skill and ease, especially a weapon or tool.

wield.e: From Middle English welde, from Old English *wield, ġewield (“power, control, dominion”), from Proto-West Germanic *waldi, from Proto-Germanic *waldiz (“power, might, control”).

wife.e: From Middle English wyf, wif, from Old English wīf (“woman, wife”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīb, from Proto-Germanic *wībą (“woman; wife”). The further etymology is unknown, with a number of disputed suggestions. One suggestion connects Tocharian A/B kip/kwīpe (“genitals, female pudenda”), for a hypothetical Indo-European *gʰwíbʰ- (“pudenda”).
wife.g: A married woman, especially in relation to her spouse.

wild.e: From Middle English weilde, wield, wielde, wijlde, wild, wilde, wyld, wylde, wyled, wyyld, from Old English wilde, from Proto-West Germanic *wilþī, from Proto-Germanic *wilþijaz (“wild”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂welh₁- (“hair; wool”).

wilderness.e: From Middle English wildernes, wildernesse (“desolate or uninhabited place, desolation”), and then either: from Middle English wilderne (“deserted or uninhabited place, wilderness; land not yet settled”) (from Old English wilddeōren (“savage, wild”); see below) + -nes, -nesse (suffix forming abstract nouns denoting qualities or states).
wilderness.g: Uncultivated and unsettled land in its natural state inhabited by wild animals and with vegetation growing wild; (countable) a tract of such

wile.e: From Middle English wile, wyle, from Old Northern French wile (“guile”) and Old English wīl (“wile, trick”) and wiġle (“divination”), from Proto-Germanic *wīlą (“craft, deceit”) (from Proto-Indo-European *wey- (“to turn, bend”)) and Proto-Germanic *wigulą, *wihulą (“prophecy”) (from Proto-Indo-European *weyk- (“to consecrate, hallow, make holy”)).
wile.g: A trick or stratagem practiced for ensnaring or deception; a sly, insidious artifice

wile.e: The phrase meaning to pass time idly is while away. We can trace the meaning in an adjectival sense for while back to Old English, hwīlen, "passing, transitory". It is also seen in whilend, "temporary, transitory". But since wile away occurs so often, it is now included in many dictionaries.
wile.g: Misspelling of while (“to pass the time”).

wilfully.e: From Old English wilfullīċe, corresponding to wilful + -ly.
wilfully.g: Willingly, of one's own free will.

will.e: From Middle English willen, wullen, wollen, from Old English willan (“to want”), from Proto-West Germanic *willjan, from Proto-Germanic *wiljaną, from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, wish”).
will.g: Used to express the future tense, sometimes with an implication of volition or determination when used in the first person. Compare shall.

will.e: From Middle English wille, from Old English willa (compare verb willian), from Proto-Germanic *wiljô (“desire, will”), from Proto-Indo-European *welh₁- (“to choose, wish”).
will.g: One's independent faculty of choice; the ability to be able to exercise one's choice or intention.

willing.e: (adjective): Old English willende, present participle of willan (noun): Old English willung, from willian By surface analysis, will + -ing.
willing.g: Ready to do something, particularly something that requires change or effort; not objecting.

willingly.e: From Middle English willyngly, wyllyngly (“intentionally, deliverately; freely, gladly”), from Old English willendlīċe (“diligently”), equivalent to willing + -ly.
willingly.g: Of one’s own free will; freely and spontaneously.

willow.e: From Middle English wilwe, welew, variant of wilghe, from Old English weliġ, from Proto-West Germanic *wilig, from Proto-Germanic *wiligaz, from Proto-Indo-European *welik- (compare (Arcadian) Ancient Greek ἑλίκη (helíkē), Hittite 𒌑𒂖𒆪 (welku, “grass”)), from *wel- (“twist, turn”).
willow.g: Any of various deciduous trees or shrubs in the genus Salix, in the willow family Salicaceae, found primarily on moist soils in cooler zones

wilt.e: From Middle English wilt, from Old English wilt, from Proto-West Germanic *wilt, second person singular preterite-present of Proto-West Germanic *willjan.

wimple.e: From Middle English wympel, wimpel, from Old English wimpel (“veil, an article of women's dress; a covering for the neck, a cloak, a hood”), from Proto-Germanic *wimpilaz (“wimple, scarf, veil”).
wimple.g: A cloth which usually covers the head and is worn around the neck and chin. It was worn by women in medieval Europe and is still worn by nun

wimple.e: From Middle English wimplen (“to cover, conceal; to fold, drape”).

win.e: From Middle English winnen, from Old English winnan (“to labour, swink, toil,”) (compare Old English ġewinnan (“conquer, obtain, gain; endure, bear, suffer; be ill”)), from Proto-West Germanic *winnan, from Proto-Germanic *winnaną (“to swink, labour, win, gain, fight”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, wish, desire, love”).

From Middle English winn, winne, from Old English winn (“toil, labor, trouble, hardship; profit, gain; conflict, strife, war”), from Proto-Germanic *winną (“labour, struggle, fight”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to strive, desire, wish, love”).

wind.e: From Middle English wynd, wind, from Old English wind (“wind”), from Proto-West Germanic *wind, from Proto-Germanic *windaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂wéh₁n̥tos (“wind”), from earlier *h₂wéh₁n̥ts (“wind”), derived from the present participle of *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”).
wind.g: Real or perceived movement of atmospheric air usually caused by convection or differences in air pressure.

wind.e: From Middle English wynden, from Old English windan, from Proto-Germanic *windaną.
wind.g: To turn coils (of a cord or something similar) around something.

windblown.g: Growing in a distorted shape produced by the prevailing winds.

winding.e: The English word is analysable as wind (“to blow air through (a wind instrument or horn) to make a sound; to cause (someone) to become breathless; to winnow (food grain), etc.”) + -ing (suffix forming present participial adjectives and verbs, and nouns denoting an action or the embodiment of an action).

window.e: From Middle English wyndowe, wyndown, from Old Norse vindauga (“window”, literally “wind-eye; wind-hole”), equivalent to wind + eye. The “windows” among early Germanic peoples were just unglazed holes (eyes) in the wall or roof that permitted wind to pass through .
window.g: An opening, usually covered by one or more panes of clear glass, to allow light and air from outside to enter a building or vehicle.

windstorm.g: A storm in which there are strong, violent winds but no precipitation.

windy.e: From Middle English windy, from Old English windiġ (“windy”), from Proto-Germanic *windigaz (“windy”), equivalent to wind + -y. The “frightened” sense probably derives from the phrase have the wind up.

windy.g: Having many bends; winding, twisting or tortuous.

wine.e: From Middle English wyn, win, from Old English wīn, from Proto-West Germanic *wīn, from Proto-Germanic *wīną, either directly or via Latin vīnum (from Proto-Italic *wīnom) from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom (“wine”).
wine.g: An alcoholic beverage made by fermenting grape juice, with an ABV ranging from 5.5–16%.

wine.e: A variant of wind with simplification of the final consonant cluster; for the vowel quality, compare find, mind, rind. The same variation of the root wind- → win- is also found in dialectal North Germanic: vind- → vin-.

winebibber.g: A habitual (or heavy) drinker of alcohol, especially wine, an excessive wine-drinker; a drunkard.

winepress.e: From Middle English wyne-presse, equivalent to wine + press.
winepress.g: A press used to extract juice from grapes as the first step of winemaking.

wineskin.g: A bag, traditionally made from the skin of a goat (a goatskin), used for holding and dispensing wine.

wing.e: From Middle English winge, wenge, from Old Norse vængr ("wing of a flying animal, wing of a building"; compare vængi (“ship's cabin”)), from Proto-Germanic *wēingijaz, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂weh₁- (“to blow”), thus related to wind. Replaced native Middle English fither (from Old English fiþre.
wing.g: An appendage of an animal's (bird, bat, insect) body that enables it to fly.

winged.e: From Middle English winged, wenged (“having wings”), past participle of wingen, from the noun winge, wenge.

wingspan.g: The distance from the left wingtip to the right wingtip (of a bird, airplane etc.).

wingtip.g: The extreme tip of the wing of an aircraft, bird, flying insect, etc.

wink.e: From Middle English wynken, from Old English wincian (“to wink, make a sign, close the eyes, blink”, weak verb), from Proto-West Germanic *winkōn (“to close one's eyes”), from Proto-Indo-European *weng- (“to bow, bend, arch, curve”).
wink.g: To close one's eyes in sleep.
Synonym of tiddlywink (“small disc used in the game of tiddlywinks”).

winnow.e: From Middle English wyndwen, from Old English windwian (“to winnow, fan, ventilate”), from Proto-West Germanic *windwōn, from Proto-Germanic *windwōną, *winþijaną (“to throw about, winnow”), from Proto-Indo-European *wē- (“to winnow, thresh”).
winnow.g: To subject (granular material, especially food grain) to a current of air separating heavier and lighter components, as grain from chaff.

winter.e: From Middle English winter, from Old English winter, from Proto-West Germanic *wintru, from Proto-Germanic *wintruz (“winter”).
winter.g: Traditionally the fourth of the four seasons, typically regarded as spanning either the period between the winter solstice to the spring equ

winterhouse.e: From Middle English winter-hous, from Old English winterhūs, equivalent to winter + house.
winterhouse.g: A house used in winter, especially as a vacation residence to overwinter in

wipe.e: From Middle English wipen, from Old English wīpian (“to wipe, rub, cleanse”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīpōn (“to wipe”), from Proto-Indo-European *weyp- (“to twist, wind around”).
wipe.g: To move an object over, maintaining contact, with the intention of removing some substance from the surface. (Compare rub.)

wipe.e: From wipe out (verb) and wipeout (noun) by shortening.
wipe.g: To have all members of a party die in a single campaign, event, or battle; to be wiped out.

wire.e: From Middle English wir, wyr, from Old English wīr (“wire, metal thread, wire-ornament”), from Proto-Germanic *wīraz (“wire”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₁iros (“a twist, thread, cord, wire”), from *weh₁y- (“to turn, twist, weave, plait”).
wire.g: Metal formed into a thin, even thread, now usually by being drawn through a hole in a steel die.

wisdom.e: From Middle English wisdom, from Old English wīsdōm (“wisdom”), from Proto-West Germanic *wīsadōm, from Proto-Germanic *wīsadōmaz (“wisdom”), corresponding to wise + -dom.
wisdom.g: An element of personal character that enables one to distinguish the wise from the unwise.

wise.e: From Middle English wys, wyse, from Old English wīs (“wise”), from Proto-Germanic *wīsaz (“knowledgeable, wise”), from Proto-Indo-European *wéydos (“seeing; knowledge”), from *weyd- (“to see”).
wise.g: Showing good judgement or the benefit of experience.

wise.e: From Middle English wise, from Old English wīse, from Proto-Germanic *wīsō.

wisely.e: From Middle English wisliche, wislike, from Old English wīslīċe (“wisely”, adverb), equivalent to wise + -ly.
wisely.g: In a wise manner; using good judgement.

wish.e: From Middle English wisshen, wischen, wüschen, from Old English wȳsċan (“to wish”), from Proto-West Germanic *wunskijan, from Proto-Germanic *wunskijaną (“to wish”), from Proto-Indo-European *wenh₁- (“to wish, love”). Via PIE cognate with Latin Venus, veneror (“venerate, honour, love”), English wonder.
wish.g: A desire, hope, or longing for something or for something to happen.

wist.e: Past indicative of wit: from Old English witan, from Proto-Germanic *witaną, from Proto-Indo-European *weyd- (“see, know”).

wit.e: From Middle English wit, witt, wyt, from Old English witt (“mind, sanity, sense, understanding”), from Proto-West Germanic *witi, from Proto-Germanic *witją (“knowledge; reason; wit”), from Proto-Germanic *witaną (“to know”), from Proto-Indo-European *wóyde (“to know”), from *weyd- (“to see”).

From Middle English witen, woten, from Old English weotan, witan, from Proto-West Germanic *witan, from Proto-Germanic *witaną (“to know”), from Proto-Indo-European *wóyde (“to know”), from *weyd- (“to see”).
wit.g: To know, be aware of (constructed with of when used intransitively).

witch.e: Possibly related to wicked; see that entry for more. The verb derives from the noun. The mathematical curve derives from a translation by John Colson of the Italian versiera, from a confusion with versoria (“rope”) and avversaria (“witch”).
witch.g: A person (now usually particularly a woman) who uses magical or supernatural powers to influence or predict events, particularly one with ma

witch.e: From Middle English wicchen, from Old English wiċċian, from Proto-Germanic *wikkōną, from Proto-Indo-European *wik-néh₂-, derivation of *weyk-.

witchcraft.e: From Middle English wicchecraft, wicchecreft, from Old English wiċċecræft, equivalent to witch + -craft.
witchcraft.g: The practice of witches; magic, sorcery, or the use of supernatural powers to influence or predict events.

with.e: From Middle English with, from Old English wiþ (“against, opposite, toward, with”), from Proto-West Germanic *wiþi, a shortened form of Proto-Germanic *wiþrą (“against”). In Middle English, the word shifted to denote association rather than opposition, displacing Middle English mid (“with”), from Old English mid (“with”), from Proto-Germanic *midi.
From Middle English withe, wiþþe, from Old English wiþþe.

withal.e: PIE word wí The adverb is derived from Middle English withal, with-al, withalle (“against, in opposition to; in association with, together with; by means of”), from with (“against; close to, near; directly opposite to; in the company of, together with; on, upon; within; etc.”, preposition) + al (“total number in a group, all, everyone, everything”).
withal.g: Together with the rest; besides; in addition.

withdraw.e: From Middle English withdrawen, withdrauen (“to depart, leave, move away; (reflexive) to go away; (reflexive) to leave someone’s service; (often reflexive) to draw back or retreat (from a battlefield or dangerous place), withdraw; to abandon, desert; to go, go forth; to move; of the sea, water, etc.: to (cause to) ebb, recede, subside; to disappear.
withdraw.g: To draw or pull (something) away or back from its original position or situation.

withdraw.e: From Middle English withdrawe (“act of stopping a judicial proceeding”), from withdrawen, withdrauen (verb): see etymology 1.
withdraw.g: An act of drawing back or removing; a removal, a withdrawal or withdrawing.

wither.e: From Middle English widren, wydderen (“to dry up, shrivel”), related to or perhaps an alteration of Middle English wederen (“to expose to weather”), from Old English wederian (“to expose to weather, exhibit a change of weather”).
wither.g: To shrivel, droop or dry up, especially from lack of water.

wither.e: From Middle English wither, from Old English wiþer (“again, against”, adverb in compounds), from Proto-West Germanic *wiþr (“against, toward”).

withers.e: From dialectal English wither (“against”) (compare wither-) + -s; see with. So-named because it is the part of the horse that pushes against a load.
withers.g: The part of the back of a four-legged animal that is between the shoulder blades; in many species the highest point of the body and the stan

withhold.e: From Middle English withholden. Equivalent to with- + hold.
withhold.g: To keep (a physical object that one has obtained) to oneself rather than giving it back to its owner.

within.e: From Middle English withinne, withinnen, from Old English wiþinnan; equivalent to with + in.
within.g: In the inner part, spatially; physically inside.

without.e: From Middle English withoute, withouten, from Old English wiþūtan (literally “against the outside of”). By surface analysis, with- + out. Superseded non-native Middle English sauns, sans (“without”), from Old French sans, sanz, senz (“without”).

withstand.e: From Middle English withstanden, from Old English wiþstandan, from Proto-West Germanic *wiþistandan (“to withstand, resist”), equivalent to with- (“against”) + stand.

witless.e: From Middle English witles, from Old English witlēas (“senseless; witless”), from Proto-Germanic *witjalausaz (“witless”), equivalent to wit + -less.

witness.e: From Middle English witnesse, from Old English ġewitnes, equivalent to wit + -ness.
witness.g: Attestation of a fact or event; testimony.

wittingly.e: From Middle English wetandly, wettanly, wetyngly, witandly, witingeliche, wittandly, wittingli, wittingly, wityngli, wityngly, witynly, wytindeliche, wytyngly, equivalent to witting + -ly.
wittingly.g: in a witting manner, intentionally, on purpose.

witty.e: From Middle English witty, witti, from Old English wittiġ, witiġ, ġewittiġ (“clever, wise”), from Proto-West Germanic *witīg, *witag, from Proto-Germanic *witagaz, *wītagaz (“knowing, wise, clever”), equivalent to wit + -y.

wizard.e: From Middle English wysard, wysarde, equivalent to wise + -ard. A uniquely medieval English word with no known morphologically exact cognates in other Germanic languages; did not gain distinct sense of "occultist, magic user" (as opposed to a philosopher or sage) until circa 1500s, aligning roughly with the starting English Renaissance.
wizard.g: Someone, usually male, who uses (or has skill with) magic, mystic items, and magical and mystical practices.
